after.name: Question 1
after.problem:
Consider the differential equation 

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x-5y-7).
$$

Using a substitution of the form $z=2x-5y,$ transform the differential equation into an equation of the form ${z}^{′}(x)=f(z).$ What is the function $f(z)?$
after.worked_solution:
First, we make the substitution

$$
z=2x-5y.
$$

Differentiating $z(x)$ using the chain rule, we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}=2-5\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}\,⟹\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\frac{2}{5}-\frac{1}{5}\,\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}.
$$

Therefore, the original equation can be written in terms of $z$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{2}{5}-\frac{1}{5}\,\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x} & =\operatorname{cos}⁡(z-7)\end{aligned}
$$

Expressing this equation in the form ${z}^{′}(x)=f(z),$ we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}=2-5\operatorname{cos}⁡(z-7).
$$

Therefore, $f(z)=2-5\operatorname{cos}⁡(z-7).$

$$

$$

after.name: Question 3
after.problem:
Consider the differential equation

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\frac{1}{3}+{e}^{x-3y+2}.
$$

 
The general solution to this equation can be expressed in the form

$$
g(x,y)=3x+C,
$$

where $C$ is a constant. What is $g(x,y)?$
after.worked_solution:
First, we make the substitution

$$
z=x-3y.
$$

Differentiating $z(x)$ using the chain rule, we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}=1-3\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}\,⟹\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\frac{1}{3}-\frac{1}{3}\,\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}.
$$

Therefore, the original equation can be written in terms of $z$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{3}-\frac{1}{3}\,\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{1}{3}+{e}^{z+2}\end{aligned}
$$

Expressing this equation in the form ${z}^{′}(x)=f(z)$ gives

$$
\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}=-3{e}^{z+2}.
$$

This differential equation is separable. So, we separate the variables and integrate both sides with respect to $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}-\frac{1}{3{e}^{z+2}}\,\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x} & =1 \\ -\frac{1}{3}\int {e}^{-(z+2)}\,\text{d}z & =\int \,\text{d}x \\ \frac{{e}^{-(z+2)}}{3} & =x+K \\ {e}^{-(z+2)} & =3x+C,\end{aligned}
$$

where $C=3K.$

Finally, we write the equation in terms of $y$ and $x$ using our original substitution, as follows:

$$
{e}^{-(x-3y+2)}=3x+C
$$

Therefore, $g(x,y)={e}^{3y-x-2}.$

decision.explanation: Set z=x+4y. Then z′=1+4y′=1/ln(z), so ln(z) dz=dx. Integration gives z ln(z)-z=x+C. Thus g(x,y)=(x+4y)(ln(x+4y)-1), option b.

after.name: Question 4
after.problem:
Consider the differential equation

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\frac{1}{4\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+4y)}-\frac{1}{4}.
$$

 
The general solution to this equation can be expressed in the form

$$
g(x,y)=x+C,
$$

where $C$ is a constant. What is $g(x,y)?$
after.worked_solution:
First, we make the substitution

$$
z=x+4y.
$$

Differentiating $z(x)$ using the chain rule, we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}=1+4\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}\,⟹\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\frac{1}{4}\,\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}-\frac{1}{4}.
$$

Therefore, the original equation can be written in terms of $z$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{4}\,\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}-\frac{1}{4} & =\frac{1}{4\operatorname{ln}⁡z}-\frac{1}{4}\end{aligned}
$$

Expressing this equation in the form ${z}^{′}(x)=f(z)$ gives

$$
\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}=\frac{1}{\operatorname{ln}⁡z}.
$$

This differential equation is separable. So, we separate the variables and integrate both sides with respect to $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{ln}⁡z\,\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x} & =1 \\ \int \operatorname{ln}⁡z\,\text{d}z & =\int \,\text{d}x\end{aligned}
$$

Using integration by parts on the left side,

$$
\begin{aligned}u=\operatorname{ln}⁡z & \,⟹\,{u}^{′}=\frac{1}{z} \\ {v}^{′}=1 & \,⟹\,v=z\end{aligned}
$$

we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \operatorname{ln}⁡z\,\text{d}z & =\int \,\text{d}x \\ z\operatorname{ln}⁡z-\int \,\text{d}z & =\int \,\text{d}x \\ z\operatorname{ln}⁡z-z & =x+C \\ z(\operatorname{ln}⁡z-1) & =x+C\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we write the equation in terms of $y$ and $x$ using our original substitution, as follows:

$$
(x+4y)(\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+4y)-1)=x+C
$$

Therefore, $g(x,y)=(x+4y)(\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+4y)-1).$

Consider the differential equation dydx=14ln⁡(x+4y)−14. The general solution to this equation can be expressed in the form g(x,y)=x+C, where C is a constant. What is g(x,y)?

a
1ln2⁡(x+4y)
b
(x+4y)(ln⁡(x+4y)−1)

x+4yln2⁡(x+4y)

(x+4y)ln⁡(x+4y)
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

First, we make the substitution z=x+4y. Differentiating z(x) using the chain rule, we get dzdx=1+4dydx⟹dydx=14dzdx−14. Therefore, the original equation can be written in terms of z as follows: 14dzdx−14=14ln⁡z−14

Expressing this equation in the form z′(x)=f(z) gives dzdx=1ln⁡z.

This differential equation is separable. So, we separate the variables and integrate both sides with respect to x:

ln⁡zdzdx=1∫ln⁡zdz=∫dx

Using integration by parts on the left side, u=ln⁡z⟹u′=1zv′=1⟹v=z

we get ∫ln⁡zdz=∫dxzln⁡z−∫dz=∫dxzln⁡z−z=x+Cz(ln⁡z−1)=x+C

Finally, we write the equation in terms of y and x using our original substitution, as follows: (x+4y)(ln⁡(x+4y)−1)=x+C

content.knowledge_point: Solving a First-Order ODE Using a Linear Substitution
content.problem:
Consider the differential equation

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\frac{1}{4\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+4y)}-\frac{1}{4}.
$$

 
The general solution to this equation can be expressed in the form

$$
g(x,y)=x+C,
$$

where $C$ is a constant. What is $g(x,y)?$
content.worked_solution:
First, we make the substitution

$$
z=x+4y.
$$

Differentiating $z(x)$ using the chain rule, we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}=1+4\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}\,⟹\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\frac{1}{4}\,\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}-\frac{1}{4}.
$$

Therefore, the original equation can be written in terms of $z$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{4}\,\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}-\frac{1}{4} & =\frac{1}{4\operatorname{ln}⁡z}-\frac{1}{4}\end{aligned}
$$

Expressing this equation in the form ${z}^{′}(x)=f(z)$ gives

$$
\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}=\frac{1}{\operatorname{ln}⁡z}.
$$

This differential equation is separable. So, we separate the variables and integrate both sides with respect to $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{ln}⁡z\,\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x} & =1 \\ \int \operatorname{ln}⁡z\,\text{d}z & =\int \,\text{d}x\end{aligned}
$$

Using integration by parts on the left side,

$$
\begin{aligned}u=\operatorname{ln}⁡z & \,⟹\,{u}^{′}=\frac{1}{z} \\ {v}^{′}=1 & \,⟹\,v=z\end{aligned}
$$

we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \operatorname{ln}⁡z\,\text{d}z & =\int \,\text{d}x \\ z\operatorname{ln}⁡z-\int \,\text{d}z & =\int \,\text{d}x \\ z\operatorname{ln}⁡z-z & =x+C \\ z(\operatorname{ln}⁡z-1) & =x+C\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we write the equation in terms of $y$ and $x$ using our original substitution, as follows:

$$
(x+4y)(\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+4y)-1)=x+C
$$

Therefore, $g(x,y)=(x+4y)(\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+4y)-1).$

\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}=6\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}-1\,⟹\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\frac{1}{6}\,\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}+\frac{1}{6}.
$$

Therefore, the original equation can be written in terms of $z$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{6}\,\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}+\frac{1}{6} & =-\operatorname{ln}⁡z\end{aligned}
$$

Expressing this equation in the form ${z}^{′}(x)=f(z),$ we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}=-6\operatorname{ln}⁡z-1.
$$

Therefore, $f(z)=-6\operatorname{ln}⁡z-1.$
